result.summary: Acheloüs tells how Erisicthon cut down Ceres' sacred oak and was punished with endless hunger sent through Famine. After he eats his fortune he sells his daughter, who escapes each time by changing shape, until he finally eats his own limbs. Acheloüs ends by noting his own limited shape-changing and his lost horn.

scenes.title: Introduction to Erisicthon's daughter
scenes.summary: A summary introduces the tale of Erisicthon and his daughter, and Acheloüs begins to speak of her.

scenes.title: The sacred oak is felled
scenes.summary: Impious Erisicthon cuts down Ceres' oak, kills a man who tries to stop him, and ignores the dying Nymph's warning.
scenes.stakes: Erisicthon risks divine punishment; the oak's Nymph and a servant lose their lives.

scenes.title: Ceres plans punishment
scenes.summary: The Dryads appeal to Ceres, who sends Oreas to Scythia to bid Famine enter Erisicthon.
scenes.stakes: Erisicthon faces deadly punishment from the goddess.

scenes.title: Oreas finds Famine
scenes.summary: Oreas flies in Ceres' dragon chariot to Caucasus in Scythia, finds gaunt Famine and delivers the order.
scenes.stakes: Oreas fears coming near Famine and feeling hunger herself.

scenes.title: Famine enters Erisicthon
scenes.summary: Famine breathes hunger into the sleeping Erisicthon, who then consumes his whole estate and sells his daughter.
scenes.stakes: Erisicthon loses his fortune and his daughter's freedom to insatiable hunger.

scenes.title: The daughter's escapes
scenes.summary: Neptune changes her into a fisherman to deceive her master; thereafter she is repeatedly sold and escapes in animal forms, while her father finally eats his own limbs.
scenes.stakes: The daughter risks slavery; Erisicthon destroys himself.

scenes.title: Acheloüs on his own changes
scenes.summary: Acheloüs says he too can change shape, but only a few times, and shows his lost horn.

alias_notes.explanation: Deo is a name for Ceres, so the oak is hers

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid double simile of ocean and fire for insatiable hunger.
Concise statement of the nature of endless appetite.

analysis.text: Impiety brings fitting punishment: the man who destroys a sacred tree is consumed by his own hunger. Metamorphosis also becomes a means of escape.
The tale reflects ancient reverence for sacred groves and the duty of honoring gods, with Ceres as guardian of agriculture.

legacy.text: Erisicthon's insatiable hunger became a classic image of greed and appetite in later literature, as in Callimachus' earlier hymn and Renaissance moralizing.

fun_facts.text: Ovid draws on an earlier version of this story in Callimachus' Hymn to Demeter, adding the daughter's shape-shifting escapes.

language_notes.text: Autolycus was a famed trickster, son of Mercury. His wife, Erisicthon's daughter, shares his gift of cunning, here the shape-changing that lets her be sold repeatedly and escape.
Fillets are ribbons or headbands, and tablets are inscribed offerings. Both were hung on sacred trees as thanks for answered prayers.
Dryads are nymphs of trees and woods. An ell is an old measure of roughly forty-five inches, so the trunk was enormous.
Triopas was Erisicthon's father. Calling him 'son of Triopas' identifies him and sets him as a Thessalian king.
'Deoïan' means belonging to Deo, another name for Ceres, so it marks the oak as the goddess's own.
'Thessalian' refers to Erisicthon, who ruled in Thessaly, a region of northern Greece.
"In black array" means the Dryads came dressed in mourning, showing grief for the felled sacred oak.
The Fates forbid Ceres, goddess of grain, to meet Famine, her opposite; this is why she must send a messenger.
Caucasus is the mountain range at the edge of the known world, here placed in Scythia, a remote northern region.
"Scurf" is flaky, scaly dry skin; here it describes Famine's cracked lips.
Hæmonia is an old name for Thessaly, in Greece, where Erisicthon lives.
"Cannot brook" means cannot endure or tolerate; "prize of my ravished virginity" refers to Neptune, who had violated her.
The master's "even so may the sea be smooth" is a courteous wish: may you be lucky, as I ask you a favor. "Credulous" means easily deceived.
Triopas was the father of Erysichthon, whom the story shows being punished with endless hunger; so the daughter is Triopas's granddaughter.
"Distemper" here means disease or disorder; the insatiable hunger sent as punishment is meant.
"O youths" addresses Acheloüs's listeners, Theseus and his companions, whom he is entertaining at his table.
Acheloüs lost a horn in his wrestling match with Hercules; this is the point of showing his forehead.

context_notes.text: Ceres (the Greek Demeter) is goddess of grain and harvest. Her sacred groves were protected, so cutting one was grave sacrilege.
Bleeding trees were a classic omen of divine anger. Sacrificial bulls were slaughtered at altars, so the comparison underlines the sacrilege.
Dryads are tree nymphs. Erisicthon had cut down Ceres' sacred oak, which housed a Dryad, and so angered the goddess.
Oreas is an oread, a mountain nymph. Ceres (the Greek Demeter) is the goddess of grain and harvest.
Neptune, god of the sea, had ravished the girl earlier, which is why she appeals to him for help.
Her father sells her to buy food; she escapes by changing form and returns, so he can sell her again.

literary_notes.text: Erisicthon is defined at once by his contempt for the gods, preparing for the punishment that follows.
The oak is said to overshadow the wood as the wood overshadows the grass, stressing its extraordinary size.
The oak shudders, groans, turns pale and sweats like a living body, revealing the sacred life within it.
Comparing the oak's flowing blood to a sacrificed bull's makes the felling a horrifying murder or profane sacrifice.
The king mocks the man's 'pious intentions' as a reward, then kills him. The dying Nymph's warning foreshadows his own fate.
Grotesque physical detail, such as a skin through which the bowels show, makes Famine's emptiness vivid and repellent.
Famine is given a body, gaunt and tearing at herbs, so an abstract force becomes a character.
Even in sleep he chews empty air, a bitter image of the futile hunger that will ruin him.
Erisicthon's hunger is compared to the sea swallowing rivers and fire consuming wood, stressing that more fuel only increases the craving.
Selling his daughter, the last thing he has, prepares for the next episode, where she escapes by shape-changing.
The master asks the disguised girl about herself, and her truthful-sounding denial deceives him; the reader enjoys what he cannot know.
Erysichthon devouring his own limbs gives a horrific, ironic end to his punishment: his hunger feeds on himself.
"Wreathed as a snake" and a herd's leader with strong horns show Acheloüs's shifting forms with vivid images.
The brief closing line returns to the frame narrator and marks the sorrow of Acheloüs for his lost horn.
